explain.say: Every year billions of birds migrate thousands of kilometres and find the same breeding grounds, sometimes even the same nest site. They combine several senses, like a navigator using several instruments.

explain.say: Young birds are born with an urge to fly in a set direction for a set time, which gets them to roughly the right area. Older birds refine the route using landmarks such as coasts and mountains, and some seabirds follow smells.

faq.q: How do birds know which way to fly?
faq.a: Birds use several compasses: the sun by day, the stars at night and Earth's magnetic field in any weather. They check these against an inborn sense of direction and, with experience, landmarks and smells.
asks: How do birds find their way south?

faq.q: How do birds use the sun to navigate?
faq.a: A bird notes where the sun is and uses its body clock to allow for the sun moving across the sky. Experiments that shifted birds' body clocks made them head off in the wrong direction by a predictable amount.
asks: Do birds use a sun compass?
How do day-flying birds find direction?

faq.q: Can birds sense Earth's magnetic field?
faq.a: Yes. In experiments, caged European robins turned to face their migration direction, and changed direction when scientists changed the magnetic field around them. How they sense it is still being studied.
asks: Do birds have a magnetic compass?

faq.q: Do young birds learn the route from their parents?
faq.a: It depends on the species. Young geese and cranes learn routes by flying with their parents, but young cuckoos fly to Africa alone, never having met their parents, guided only by instinct.
asks: Is bird migration learned or instinct?
How do young birds know where to go?

faq.q: How far do migrating birds fly?
faq.a: Some fly astonishing distances. A bar-tailed godwit tracked in 2022 flew about 13,560 kilometres nonstop from Alaska to Tasmania in 11 days, without eating or resting.
asks: What is the longest nonstop bird flight?
How long can birds fly without stopping?

facts: Caged European robins orient using Earth's magnetic field (Wiltschko and Wiltschko, 1972).
Young common cuckoos migrate from Europe to Africa alone, without ever meeting their parents.
